summary: Aaliyah finds Duolingo helpful for casual Italian learning but wishes it better addressed conversational skills needed to connect with her boyfriend's family.
top_quotes: Duolingo is fab for the basics, but when it comes to having a real chat with my boyfriend's nonna, I feel like a fish out of water.
Honestly, those streaks keep me coming back even when I can't be arsed.
I reckon if Duolingo added more speaking practice, I'd be fluent by now.

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Hey, how's it going? I'm Aaliyah, nice to chat with you!

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Right, so I'm from London, 26, and I work in marketing. I'm learning Italian 'cause my boyfriend's family is from Italy, you know? Anyway, grew up here, and life's been a mix of hustle and trying to enjoy the little things. Love traveling, love a cheeky night out with mates, and lately, I'm all about mastering Italian so I can impress his folks!

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up in East London, right amid all the buzz and hustle. It's a proper melting pot of cultures.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: It was lively, you know? There's always something happening. Loads of different foods, languages. Quite fast-paced, but also there’s a real sense of community. You know, neighbors looking out for each other kind of vibe.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: I guess a big turning point was getting into marketing after uni. I'd done a degree in business, but wasn’t sure what direction to take. Landed an internship, and the rest is history. Really opened my eyes to what I could do and what I wanted, you know?

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Well, I finally felt like I was on a path that suited me. It was exciting, creative, and just the right amount of challenging. It taught me a lot about myself, like discovering I actually love connecting with people and telling stories through marketing.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: I just dove in headfirst, to be honest. Was a bit daunting, but I knew I had to give it a go. Asked loads of questions, networked, and really put myself out there. Turns out, taking those opportunities really paid off.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, I’d say connecting with my boyfriend’s family is a big one. Plus, really pushing my career a step further. But yeah, learning Italian is a biggie, especially because his family means a lot to him and I want to be part of that.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: It’s important 'cause I want to be more than just that ‘girlfriend’ who can’t engage with his family. Being able to speak their language, it’s about respect and showing them I care. Also, career-wise, I want to make sure I'm always moving forward.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day? Probably starts with a lie-in, then maybe brunch with some mates. Could be a productive day at work where everything just clicks, you know? Wrapping it up with a cosy evening in, maybe a bit of Duolingo practice or Netflix. Simple things.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: If I feel like I’ve got a nice balance of getting stuff done and having a bit of fun or relaxation. Plus, if I manage a decent convo in Italian, that’s always a win!

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: Big decisions, I usually weigh the pros and cons quite a bit. I'll talk it over with people I trust, like my mum or my boyfriend. Sometimes a bit of a gut reaction too, you know? If something feels right or wrong, I listen to that.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: Definitely a bit of both, really. I like having a rough plan, but I’m not too bothered if things change. Sort of go-with-the-flow within reason, if you get me.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Last holiday, for instance, we planned to visit Rome but didn’t have a strict itinerary. Ended up stumbling into this lovely local market which wasn’t planned but was one of the highlights! I love those spontaneous moments.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: Pretty cautiously, I'd say. I mean, I'm not afraid to take risks, but I like to know what I’m getting into. I'll usually think it through, talk it over with someone, and if the risk seems worth it, I’ll go for it.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: Weekdays are pretty standard. Wake up, coffee to get me going, then off to work. Spend the day on campaigns, meetings. After work, might hit the gym if I’m feeling it, but often I’ll just chill, do a bit of Italian on Duolingo or catch up with my boyfriend. Dinner, some telly, and sort of wind down from there.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Definitely the workday. It’s lots of thinking on your feet, keeping up with tasks, and making sure everything’s on track with projects. By the end, I’m usually a bit knackered, needing some recharge time.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I wish I had more time for Italian conversations with real people. Also, just leisure stuff—travelling, new hobbies, trying new things. Seems like there’s never enough hours in the day!

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, time management was a biggie. Working from home blurred lines between work and personal time, and I felt like I was always juggling. It was a bit overwhelming at times.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I started setting more boundaries, like a clear end to my workday. Planned more for my free time, too, making sure I had time for language practice and family. It helped loads in feeling more balanced.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: My boyfriend, definitely, and my mum. I’ve got a tight circle of friends too. They’re the kind of people you can always rely on, you know? Proper support system.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: They’re really supportive and grounding. My boyfriend’s my best friend, my partner in everything. Mum’s always got my back, and my friends are, well, like my chosen family.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Mostly at home, especially these days. Then work, obviously. Whenever I can, I’m out and about in the city, finding new spots to hang out.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: Comfortable at home, it’s like my sanctuary. Work can be a bit stressful but also exciting. When I’m out in the city, it’s a bit of freedom, you know? Love the energy.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: Home is where I can relax and be me. Work, well, it keeps me on my toes. And the city’s just got this vibe that’s like nowhere else.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: I usually talk to my boyfriend first, then my mum if I need more advice. They’re both great at listening and giving a different perspective. Sometimes it’s nice to just have them hear me out, you know?

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: I’d say when my work project didn’t go as planned. We put loads of effort in, but it just didn’t hit the mark. Felt like a personal knock, you know?

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: Made me feel a bit rubbish, I won’t lie. Like, what could I have done differently? But it also sort of motivated me to do better next time, be more prepared.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: Talked it over with my team, learned from it. Then at home, I just took a bit of time to unwind. Sometimes I’d just chat with the boyfriend, watch something silly, or distract myself with a bit of Duolingo practice. Helped clear my head a bit.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Definitely stepping back from whatever’s stressing me out. Bit of a breather, you know? Going for a walk or listening to some music helps, and talking it out with someone who gets it.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: I’d love to be more settled career-wise, maybe a director position or launching my own thing. Fluent in Italian for sure, and more travelled. I just want to feel like I’m living fully, you know? With my boyfriend, maybe start a family, who knows?

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: More balance between work and life, and feeling more connected with my boyfriend’s family language-wise. Just more time to enjoy things instead of rushing about.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: I tried those language books and CDs, even a few YouTube vids. But it was hard to stick with it, you know? I’d start and stop, and it felt like I wasn’t getting anywhere. Needed something that fit into my day better.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: Definitely the lack of interaction. I mean, how many times can you listen to a CD before losing your marbles? And the books felt too textbook-y, if you know what I mean. Needed something engaging.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: I remember trying to chat with my boyfriend’s mum, and I completely blanked. Felt like all that book learning went out the window. That’s when I knew I needed something else. Something more practical.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I actually heard about it from a mate at work. She was using it for Spanish and couldn’t stop raving about how easy and fun it was. Thought I’d give it a go after that.

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: The whole gamification bit, honestly. The idea of earning streaks and levelling up made it feel less like a chore and more like a game. Plus, it’s all on my phone, so I could practice anywhere.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Right, so the other day I pulled it up on my phone after dinner. Opened the app, checked out my streak—can’t lose that now! Did a few exercises on Italian verbs, then some vocabulary practice. I like how it’s all broken into small, manageable bits. Ended with one of those speaking exercises. Having Duolingo talk back is always a laugh when I get it wrong and it corrects me, you know?

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: Definitely the immediate feedback. Like, when I mess up a word and it tells me right there. Plus, the reminders to practice are a lifesaver, especially when I’m forgetful or busy.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Probably the lack of real conversation practice. I mean, the exercises are great, but I often feel like I’m just repeating phrases. Would be awesome if it had more interactive speaking bits.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: Sometimes it feels a bit repetitive, you know? Like I’m nailing the basics over and over, but not really advancing in terms of real-world conversation. Can feel a bit like I’m stuck in a loop.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, last time I was at my boyfriend’s family dinner, I realised I knew loads of words but couldn’t string them into a proper sentence. Made me see that while Duolingo’s great for vocabulary, I need more practice actually speaking. Felt a bit embarrassed, to be honest.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, sometimes I’ll watch Italian films with subtitles or try conversation exchange apps. It helps, ‘cause I get to hear the language naturally and try forming my own sentences. Sort of fills in the gaps, you know?

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: They give me real-world practice. Hearing how Italians actually speak, picking up on slang or expressions that don’t always show up in the app. It’s more about the flow of conversation, which Duolingo doesn’t quite capture yet.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Worst case, I suppose, is getting stuck at a beginner level and never really being able to hold proper conversations with the family. You can imagine how awkward that’d be, just kind of smiling and nodding all the time.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it gives me a quick but effective session. Something that'll stick, you know? Maybe even surprise me with a new lesson or a tip that clicks. Always hoping for that little 'aha' moment.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: If I can recall the words and use them outside the app. Like if I remember a phrase when I’m trying to chat in Italian at a café or with my boyfriend’s family, then it’s definitely worked.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: Definitely more speaking practice. Maybe some prompts or interactive dialogues to help with natural conversation. It’d be a game changer for sure.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: Making language learning a bit more immersive, like having more opportunities for interaction with native speakers without needing to travel. Would love more real-world application.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: Not really, nah. I think we got most of it. Just that I’m glad there’s something like Duolingo to make learning a bit more accessible, you know?

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Sure, sounds interesting! As long as it helps improve the app, I’m all for it!
